newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Endemol seeks to consolidate TV strength.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Endemol seeks to consolidate TV strength.

text.p: Endemol NV, already a leading European TV production group, said on Thursday it planned to further consolidate its position by acquiring a production firm in a major European country soon.

Chief financial officer Aat Schouwenaar told Reuters in an interview that Endemol was already one of the top players in its field in the Netherlands, Germany and Spain and was keen to obtain similar status in Britain, Italy and France.
"We will be making an announcement about an acquisition in at least one of those three countries," he said.
"Our strategy in the coming years is to obtain a strong position in the larger European countries," Schouwenaar said.
Acquisitions would probably continue to take the form of a substantial minority stake with an option for Endemol to expand this to a majority holding at a later date, he said.

Schouwenaar said Endemol planned to exploit its size and economies of scale to build up a network of European production companies, enabling it to take a programme which had proved successful in one country and market it all over the continent.
"We plan to use the advantage we already have in Europe to obtain a position which will be difficult for others to reach."
Schouwenaar said Endemol was one of Europe's top two independent television production companies with 1996 TV production revenes of some 500 million guilders ($257.2 million).
The only other European company with TV production revenues on that scale is Pearson Plc through its Thames and Grundy subsidiaries, Schouwenaar said.
Independent TV production was still a fairly young industry in Europe, he said, with leading firms in many countries attaining annual sales of no more than 50-100 million guilders.
Endemol has developed game show formats which have become big prime-time hits in the Netherlands and which have proved just as successful when produced locally for other markets.

In the past Endemol has allowed other companies to adapt and produce its formats for markets outside the Netherlands and Germany, but Schouwenaar said this task would increasingly be performed by local Endemol subsidiaries.
"That means we earn more money and we keep tighter control of the format," he said.
Schouwenaar said Endemol expected to restore deflated investor confidence in the company which has led to marked underperformance of its share price on the Amsterdam bourse.
The company reported a 19 percent first-half profit rise on April 8 but its share price fell sharply and has remained under pressure because analysts had been looking for more.

After peaking at over 63 guilders just before the first-half results, the shares have since slumped back to around 48 guilders -- a drop of about 23 percent in a period when Amsterdam's AMX mid-cap index has risen 17 percent.
"Confidence was damaged but I'm convinced we will be able to restore that confidence in the coming months," he said.
Schouwenaar said with the benefit of hindsight the company now realised it was partly to blame for not signalling to analysts before the results that their estimates were too high.

But he said he was not too worried by the underperformance of the company's shares and believed the share price would recover, as long as Endemol delivered on last year's promise of sustained profit growth.
"We are staying with our forecast of profit growth of 15 to 20 percent this year...and our long-term vision of a doubling of turnover and profits in five years," he said.
Schouwenaar said Endemol expected to sign a new three-year contract with German broadcaster RTL Television -- a major customer -- by the end of September.

A report in Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf in April suggested that negotiations with RTL were likely to lead to a far less lucrative deal for Endemol, and although the company contested this, it added to pressure on its share price.
